hook: At a farmers market, the price of strawberries settles each morning at the point where what shoppers want matches what growers brought. When a heat wave cuts the harvest, that meeting point moves. Most exam graphs ask the same thing: where do the curves cross, and where do they cross after one of them moves?

prereq.q: Buyers' incomes rise and they want more of a good at every price. On the graph, D
options: stays put while you move along it
prereq.why: A change off the axes shifts the curve; more wanted at every price is a shift right.

prereq.q: An upward-sloping curve shows that as price rises, quantity
prereq.why: Upward sloping means both rise together.

figure.caption: The curves cross at E1. After S shifts left to S2, they cross at E2: a higher price (P2) and a smaller quantity (Q2).

chain.cause: Two curves cross at one point
chain.effect: that point gives the one price and quantity both curves agree on (E1)
the crossing moves along the other curve to a new point (E2)

chain.cause: You draw dashed lines from E1 and E2 to both axes
chain.effect: you can compare the old and new price and quantity

chain.cause: You state each change with its direction
chain.effect: "the price rises from P1 to P2" earns the point

ideas: The intersection point is where two curves cross: on a market graph, the price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer.
When one curve shifts, the crossing slides along the curve that did not move.
A before-and-after comparison marks both crossings, E1 and E2, with dashed lines to both axes (P1, P2, Q1, Q2) and says which way each moved.

misconception.wrong: When a curve shifts right, the new crossing is always higher.
misconception.right: It depends on which curve moved. D shifting right slides up the upward curve S (higher price); S shifting right slides down the downward curve D (lower price). Follow the curve that did not move.

summary: Where two curves cross, they agree on one price and one quantity. When one curve shifts, the crossing slides along the other curve to a new point. Mark both crossings with dashed lines to both axes, label the old and new values, and state the direction of each change: that before-and-after comparison is what readers score on every graph in the course.
